pages.title: Georgia at the 2026 Winter Olympics - Wikipedia
passages: | Competitors | 8 (4 men and 4 women) in 2 sports |

[Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country) "Georgia (country)") competed at the [2026 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Winter_Olympics "2026 Winter Olympics") in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") and [Cortina d'Ampezzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortina_d'Ampezzo "Cortina d'Ampezzo"), Italy, from 6 to 22 February 2026.

The Georgian team consisted of eight athletes (four per gender) competing in two sports: alpine skiing and figure skating.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Figure skaters [Luka Berulava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luka_Berulava "Luka Berulava") and [Diana Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Davis "Diana Davis") were the country's flagbearer during the [opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Winter_Olympics_opening_ceremony "2026 Winter Olympics opening ceremony").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Meanwhile, [Luka Berulava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luka_Berulava "Luka Berulava") and [Nino Tsiklauri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nino_Tsiklauri "Nino Tsiklauri") were the country's flagbearer during the [closing ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Winter_Olympics_closing_ceremony "2026 Winter Olympics closing ceremony").[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

On 16 February, [Luka Berulava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luka_Berulava "Luka Berulava") and [Anastasiia Metelkina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasiia_Metelkina "Anastasiia Metelkina") won the silver medal in the [figure skating pairs event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating_at_the_2026_Winter_Olympics_–_Pair_skating "Figure skating at the 2026 Winter Olympics – Pair skating"), marking the country's first ever [Winter Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic "Winter Olympic") medal.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Main articles: [Figure skating at the 2026 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating_at_the_2026_Winter_Olympics "Figure skating at the 2026 Winter Olympics") and [Figure skating at the 2026 Winter Olympics – Qualification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating_at_the_2026_Winter_Olympics_–_Qualification "Figure skating at the 2026 Winter Olympics – Qualification")

In the [2025 World Figure Skating Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_World_Figure_Skating_Championships "2025 World Figure Skating Championships") in Boston, the United States, Georgia secured one quota in each of the men's singles, the pair skating, and the ice dance.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Georgia earned one quota in women's singles at the [ISU Skate to Milano Figure Skating Qualifier 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISU_Skate_to_Milano "ISU Skate to Milano") in Beijing, China.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) Furthermore, Georgia qualified to the team event.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

pages.title: Georgia men's national ice hockey team - Wikipedia
passages: A trainer from Moscow, Valentin Zakharov, was sent to Georgia to train youth in the sport.

As [Tbilisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tbilisi "Tbilisi"), the capital, had no rink, most of the initial exercises involved dry-land training.[[4]](#cite_note-One_life-4) As the [Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic"), Georgia played its first game in 1962 during the [Winter Spartakiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartakiad "Spartakiad") which was held in [Sverdlovsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yekaterinburg "Yekaterinburg"), [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").

In October 2015 Georgia participated in the first game of the [2018 Winter Olympic qualification tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_hockey_at_the_2018_Winter_Olympics_–_Men's_qualification "Ice hockey at the 2018 Winter Olympics – Men's qualification"), against [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Bulgaria men's national ice hockey team"), losing the match 9–1.[[14]](#cite_note-14) Funding from the Georgian government came for the first time in 2015; prior to that the players and management had to pay all expenses.[[9]](#cite_note-Qarsthusli-9) In the [2016 Division III tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IIHF_World_Championship_Division_III "2016 IIHF World Championship Division III"), they finished second after winning four games out of five, only losing to [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Turkey men's national ice hockey team") 5–4, and having the tournament's leading scorer, Boris Kochkin (who had 10 goals and 9 assists).[[15]](#cite_note-15) However, all their matches were later nullified and the results recorded as 5–0 forfeits due to Georgia's use of ineligible players.[[16]](#cite_note-2016_ineligible-16) At the [2017 Division III tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_IIHF_World_Championship_Division_III "2017 IIHF World Championship Division III") they placed third, winning three of their five games.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Five Georgians placed in the top ten scorers, including Artem Kozyulin in first with 25 points (13 goals and 12 assists), while Artem Kurbatov was named the tournament's best defeceman.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19) In the [2018 Division III tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_IIHF_World_Championship_Division_III "2018 IIHF World Championship Division III"), they finished first after winning four games out of five, losing one game to South Africa 4–2.

Five of the top ten scorers in the tournament were from the Georgian team, including Aleksandr Zhuzhunashvili, who led the tournament in goals (10), assists (9), and points (19), and was named the best forward.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) For the first time, Georgia earned promotion to [Division IIB for 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IIHF_World_Championship_Division_II "2019 IIHF World Championship Division II").

The result was attributed to a policy of [naturalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization "Naturalization"): three of the top five scorers had Russian or Ukrainian surnames, while all five learned hockey outside of Georgia.[[22]](#cite_note-22) The result had Georgia place 40th in the [IIHF World Ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IIHF_World_Ranking "IIHF World Ranking"), their highest spot to date.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

pages.title: Olympedia – 2026 Winter Olympics Overview
passages: The 2026 Olympic Winter Games were held in northern Italy, ostensibly in Milano and Cortina d’Ampezzo, but these Games were the most spread-out Olympics ever.
They were Italy’s third Olympic Winter Games, after Cortina d’Ampezzo 1956 and Torino 2006.
Milano-Cortina, or MiCo26, as it was often referred to, was awarded the 2026 Winter Olympics in June 2019 at the 134th IOC Session, defeating a bid from Stockholm-Åre, Sweden, by a vote of 47-34.

It was the first vote decided by the new IOC system for selecting host cities in which the IOC started dialogues with various cities, but then whittled down the candidates, and effectively chose the host city almost by acclamation.

Five other cities had made overtures for the 2026 Winter Olympics, including Calgary, Alberta, Canada; Erzurum, Turkey; Sapporo, Japan; Graz, Austria; and Sion, Switzerland, but all of them either withdrew their bid or were not invited to the final IOC vote.
The IOC had also mandated that future host cities had to use existing facilities, which meant that the 2026 Winter Olympics had to be spread across most of northern Italy.
There were four main clusters – Milano, Cortina, Livigno, and Predrazzo.
While this saved on facility costs, it gave the 2026 Winter Olympics a different feel, as the athletes, the spectators, and the media were spread far and wide.
Someone who wanted to see an event in Milano and Cortina would have an 8-10 hour travel time.
Another venue concern involved the secondary ice hockey rink in Milano, the PalaItalia Santa Giulia.
This one was barely finished on time, and not all the amenities in the facility were complete, but the ice and rink seemed fine and there were no complaints from the players.
He became the first Winter Olympian to win six gold medals at a single celebration, surpassing [Eric Heiden](/athletes/86551)’s mark of five golds at Lake Placid 1980 in speed skating.

Klæbo added to his medal totals from the 2018 and 2022 Winter Olympics, leaving Italy with 13 medals and 11 gold medals, the second most gold medals of any Olympian, winter or summer, after [Michael Phelps](/athletes/93860)’ 23.
The top medalist on the women’s side was French biathlete [Julia Simon](/athletes/148329), who won three gold medals and added a silver.

Another notable performance came in Alpine skiing as Switzerland’s [Franjo von Allmen](/athletes/157056) won the men’s downhill, super-G, and the men’s team combined, becoming only the fourth Alpine skier to win three gold medals at a single Winter Olympics, following [Toni Sailer](/athletes/97080) (1956), [Jean-Claude Killy](/athletes/87932) (1968), and [Janica Kostelić](/athletes/99432) (2002).

Norway dominated the medal tables, setting Winter Olympic records for the most golds (18) and most medals (41) won at a single celebration, breaking their own records from PyeongChang 2018, when they won 39 medals, and Beijing 2022, with 16 gold medals.
Most of the Norwegian success came on the men’s side, where they won 14 gold medals.
There were 70 nations who had female competitors.
Of these, 30 nations won medals, with Brazil and Georgia winning their first ever Winter Olympic medals.
Twenty nations won gold medals, including Brazil, as [Lucas Pinheiro Braathen](/athletes/148687), who had competed in 2022 for Norway, won the Alpine skiing giant slalom for their first gold medal.
These were the biggest Olympic Winter Games ever, with 116 events – 54 for men, 50 for women, and 12 mixed events.
The gender difference was mostly due to Nordic combined as women still did not compete in that discipline at the Olympics.
There were over 2,800 competitors for the first time, with almost equal numbers among men and women, the differences being the Nordic combined and more and larger squads in ice hockey.
There was one new sporting discipline, as ski mountaineering débuted on the Olympic Programme with three events, a sprint event for men, a sprint event for women, and a mixed relay.
Overall, the Milano-Cortina 2026 Olympic Winter Games were highly successful, with only minimal controversies, and nothing that disrupted the competitions.
The Games were different because of their spread-out nature, but that may be a harbinger of future Winter Olympics because of the necessity of having multiple special venues.

pages.title: Ice hockey at the 2026 Winter Olympics – Men's tournament - Wikipedia
passages: The men's tournament in [ice hockey at the 2026 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_hockey_at_the_2026_Winter_Olympics "Ice hockey at the 2026 Winter Olympics") took place in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), Italy, between 11 and 22 February 2026.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Twelve countries [qualified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_hockey_at_the_2026_Winter_Olympics_–_Men's_qualification "Ice hockey at the 2026 Winter Olympics – Men's qualification") for the tournament; eight via [ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IIHF_World_Ranking "IIHF World Ranking") by the [IIHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Ice_Hockey_Federation "International Ice Hockey Federation"), three via qualification tournaments, and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Italy men's national ice hockey team") as hosts. [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Russia men's national ice hockey team") and [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Belarus men's national ice hockey team") were banned from competing due to the countries' [invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022–present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "United States men's national ice hockey team") won their first gold medal since [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_hockey_at_the_1980_Winter_Olympics "Ice hockey at the 1980 Winter Olympics"), defeating [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Canada men's national ice hockey team") 2–1 in [overtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_(ice_hockey) "Overtime (ice hockey)") in the gold medal game.[[4]](#cite_note-4) [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Finland men's national ice hockey team"), the defending [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_hockey_at_the_2022_Winter_Olympics_–_Men's_tournament "Ice hockey at the 2022 Winter Olympics – Men's tournament") Olympic champions,[[5]](#cite_note-5) were defeated by Canada in the semifinals[[6]](#cite_note-6) and won the bronze medal over 2022 bronze medalists [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia_men's_national_ice_hockey_team "Slovakia men's national ice hockey team").[[7]](#cite_note-7)

pages.title: Olympedia – Georgia (GEO)
passages: The National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Georgia was formed in 1989 and recognized by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) at the IOC session in Monte Carlo, in September 1993.
Georgia first competed at the 1996 Summer Games as an independent nation.
Georgia has won 40 Olympic medals, with 10 gold, all at the Summer Olympics.

One athlete from Georgia has won two gold medals: [Lasha Talakhadze](/athletes/134095), in 2016 and 2020, both in the weightlifting super-heavyweight class. [Lasha Shavdatuashvili](/athletes/121786) is the only Georgian athlete with three medals, one of each color, in men’s judo half-lightweight (2012) and lightweight classes (2016 and 2020).
Georgia’s first Olympic appearance as an independent nation occurred at Lillehammer 1994, where it was represented by five athletes who competed in luge, alpine skiing, and ski jumping.
It has since competed at all eight Olympic Winter Games through 2022, with its athletes having competed in Alpine skiing, figure skating, luge, and ski jumping.
